title: Against a 'virtual and implicit' love of God in the ignorant
source_text: XIV. Caeterum frustra hic distinguunt nonnulli quendam amorem Dei virtualem atque implicitum, ab amore Dei formali atque explicito: quasi aliquis Deum formaliter non diligens, imo Deum ignorans, censeri tamen posset illum implicite amare, cum diligit actiones quasdam a Deo praeceptas, quae hoc ipso Deo placere censendae sunt. Nam qui Deum ignorat, aut non operatur ex Dei amore, vel actuali vel habituali, proculdubio ex sui amore operatur, ac seipsum supra omnia diligit; nec actionem honestam diligit, nisi ut ea gaudeat, atque sibi placeat. Omnis vero sui amor qui divino non subordinatur, vitiosus & peccaminosus est. In amore autem aliquo vitioso laudabilem quendam Dei amorem implicitum esse, prorsus est contra rationem.
pass_a_gloss: XIV. But in vain here some distinguish a certain virtual and implicit love of God, from formal and explicit love of God: as if someone not formally loving God, nay ignorant of God, could yet be deemed to love him implicitly, when he loves certain actions by God commanded, which by this very fact are to be deemed to please God. For he who is ignorant of God, or does not work from the love of God, either actual or habitual, without doubt works from love of self, and loves himself above all things; nor does he love an honest action, except that he may rejoice in it, and please himself. But every love of self which to the divine is not subordinated, is vicious and sinful. But in some vicious love a certain laudable implicit love of God to be, is altogether against reason.
pass_b_english: Thesis XIV. It is useless for some to distinguish here between a virtual, implicit love of God and a formal, explicit one, as though someone who does not formally love God, and is even ignorant of him, could still be reckoned to love him implicitly when he loves certain actions God has commanded, actions that must for that very reason be reckoned pleasing to God.

For whoever does not know God, or does not act from love of God, whether actual or habitual, undoubtedly acts from love of himself and loves himself above all things. He loves an upright action only so that he may take joy in it and be pleased with himself. Every love of self not subordinated to the love of God is vicious and sinful, and it is wholly unreasonable to find a praiseworthy implicit love of God inside a vicious love.
